A report from CommBank iQ, a joint venture between the Commonwealth Bank and data ﬁrm Quantium Group, has found that the spending gap is widening between younger and older Australians, with those in their mid-to-late-twenties most affected by relentless price rises. The 25- to 29-year-old cohort cut their spending by 3.5% in the March quarter compared with last year. When inﬂation is added, consumption shrank more than 7%, with spending in almost all categories including essential items falling. “For these Australians, a cutback in travel, household goods and apparel expenditure was paired with lower spending on supermarkets and utilities, ” the report said. text: ECONOMICS UNIT 0–1 经济学导论 · 完整课堂笔记 Introduction to Economics | Microeconomics · Foundation Studies 知识笔记 · 英文整段 + 中文整段 · 核心重点 · 例题应用 · 重点课件原图 内容依据：Lecture 1.1–1.2、Tutorial 1、Unit 1 Tutorial Guide。Unit 0 的课程欢迎与行政说明不包含独立经济学理论，因此不重复收录。 KEY POINT 重点｜Scarcity is the central economic problem: unlimited wants must be satisfied using limited resources. 稀缺性是经济学的核心问题：人类欲望无限，但可供使用的资源有限。 Economics, Economy and Economic Activity｜经济学、经济与经济活动 Economics｜经济学 Economics is the study of how individuals, businesses and societies organise and allocate scarce resources to produce goods and services and satisfy unlimited wants. It examines choices, the use of resources and the consequences of different decisions. 经济学研究个人、企业和社会如何组织与分配稀缺资源，以生产商品和服务并满足无限的欲望。它关注人们如何做出选择、如何使用资源，以及不同决策产生的后果。 KEY POINT 重点｜Economics focuses on choices made under scarcity. 经济学重点研究稀缺条件下的选择。 An Economy｜经济 An economy is the system through which scarce resources are organised and used to produce, distribute, exchange and consume goods and services. An economy may be considered at the level of a city, country or the world. 经济是一个组织和使用稀缺资源、完成商品和服务的生产、分配、交换与消费的体系。经济可以是一个城市、一个国家或整个世界范围内的经济活动。 EXAMPLE 例题｜The coffee shop economy A coffee shop purchases coffee beans and milk, employs workers, produces drinks and sells them to customers. Suppliers earn revenue, employees receive wages and customers obtain drinks. These connected activities are part of an economy. 一家咖啡店采购咖啡豆和牛奶、雇用员工、制作饮料并销售给顾客。供应商获得收入，员工获得工资，顾客获得饮料。这些相互联系的活动构成经济的一部分。 Goods and Services｜商品与服务 Goods are tangible products that people can purchase and use, such as food, clothing and phones. Services are intangible activities provided to consumers, such as tutoring, delivery and medical treatment. Both goods and services are produced using scarce resources. 商品是人们能够购买和使用的有形产品，例如食品、衣服和手机。服务是提供给消费者的无形活动，例如家教、配送和医疗。商品和服务都需要使用稀缺资源进行生产。 Concept 概念 Distinguishing feature 区别 Example 例子 Economics 经济学 The study of allocation and choice / 对选择与分配的研究 Why rents rise / 为什么租金上涨 Economy 经济 The real system of economic activity / 实际经济活动体系 Australian economy / 澳大利亚经济 Goods 商品 Tangible / 有形 Bread, computer / 面包、电脑 Services 服务 Intangible / 无形 Teaching, delivery / 教学、配送 Scarcity and the Basic Economic Problem｜稀缺性与基本经济问题 Scarcity｜稀缺性 Scarcity occurs when the resources available are insufficient to satisfy all human wants. Resources include natural materials, human time and skills, machinery and entrepreneurial ability. Because resources are limited, people cannot obtain every good and service they would like. 当可利用的资源不足以满足人类所有欲望时，就出现稀缺性。资源包括自然资源、人的时间和技能、机器设备以及企业家能力。由于资源有限，人们无法获得自己想要的全部商品和服务。 Lecture 1.1 · Page 14 — The economic problem（无限欲望与稀缺资源） KEY POINT 重点｜Unlimited wants + limited resources → scarcity → choices. 无限欲望 + 有限资源 → 稀缺性 → 必须做出选择。 Scarcity Applies to Everyone｜稀缺性影响所有人 Scarcity affects individuals and nations regardless of how wealthy they are. A person with little money must choose which necessities to purchase, while a wealthy person still has limited time and financial resources relative to all possible projects. Even a person who deliberately leads a simple life must allocate limited time and resources. 无论贫富，个人和国家都会受到稀缺性的影响。收入有限的人必须决定优先购买哪些必需品；富有的人相对于所有可能的项目而言，仍然拥有有限的时间和资金。即使刻意过简朴生活，也需要分配有限的时间和资源。 EXAMPLE 例题｜Monks and wealthy donors A monk may choose to spend an hour studying rather than working, because time is limited. A wealthy donor cannot fund every environmental project and must decide which projects receive money. Both face scarcity. 一名僧人可能选择用一小时学习而不去工作，因为时间有限。一位富有的捐赠者无法资助所有环保项目，必须决定把资金分配给哪些项目。两者都面临稀缺性。 Scarcity versus Shortage｜稀缺性与短缺的区别 EXTENSION 补充知识｜Scarcity is a permanent condition arising from limited resources and extensive wants. A shortage is a market situation in which the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied at a particular price. A shortage may disappear if the price or supply conditions change, but scarcity does not disappear simply because a market clears. 稀缺性是由资源有限、欲望广泛而产生的长期基本状态。短缺是特定价格下需求量大于供给量的市场现象。价格或供给状况变化后，市场短缺可能消失；但即使市场达到均衡，资源稀缺性仍然存在。 EXAMPLE 例题｜Scarcity or shortage? Water is scarce because obtaining and purifying usable water requires limited resources. If supermarkets temporarily sell out of bottled water during a sudden surge in demand, that is a shortage at the prevailing price. 水具有稀缺性，因为获取和净化可用水需要有限资源。如果超市因突然增加的需求而暂时售罄瓶装水，这属于当前价格下发生的短缺。 Needs, Wants and Choice｜需要、欲望与选择 EXTENSION 补充知识｜Needs are essentials for survival and basic wellbeing, while wants are goods or experiences that people desire beyond those essentials. Economic decisions commonly involve choosing between competing wants and uses of limited time, income and resources. The distinction between needs and wants can depend on circumstances. 需要是生存和基本生活所必需的条件，而欲望还包括人们希望拥有的其他商品或体验。经济决策通常要求人们在有限时间、收入和资源的不同用途之间进行取舍。需要与欲望的具体界限也会因情境而不同。 KEY POINT 重点｜Having money does not eliminate scarcity; it only changes the choices available. 拥有更多金钱不会消除稀缺性，只会改变可供选择的方案。 Choice, Trade-offs and Opportunity Cost｜选择、权衡与机会成本 Why Choices Are Necessary｜为什么必须选择 Whenever a scarce resource has more than one possible use, choosing one option means giving up another. Households allocate income between consumption and saving; businesses allocate labour and equipment between products; governments allocate public funds between competing services. 当一种稀缺资源有多种用途时，选择一个方案就意味着放弃另一个方案。家庭在消费与储蓄之间分配收入，企业在不同产品之间分配劳动力和设备，政府在不同公共服务之间分配财政资金。 Trade-offs and Opportunity Cost｜权衡与机会成本 EXTENSION 补充知识｜A trade-off arises when obtaining more of one thing requires accepting less of another. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best alternative forgone when a choice is made. It is not necessarily the amount of money spent; time and other sacrificed opportunities may also have value. Opportunity cost is developed more fully in the next unit. 权衡是指为了得到更多某种东西，必须接受另一个方面的减少。机会成本是做出选择时放弃的次优替代方案的价值。它不一定等于实际支付的金钱，时间和放弃的其他机会也可能有价值。机会成本会在下一单元继续深入学习。 EXAMPLE 例题｜Study or work A student has two available hours and can either study economics or earn $60 from tutorin

Scarcity and the Three Fundamental Questions | 稀缺性与三个基本经济问题 Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem: resources are limited, while human wants are unlimited. Economies must therefore choose how to allocate resources. Choosing more of one good can mean producing less of another. 稀缺性是经济学的基本问题：资源有限，而人的欲望无限。因此经济体必须选择如何分配资源。多生产一种商品，可能意味着另一种商品的产量减少。 1.1 What to produce? | 生产什么？ Every economy must decide which goods and services to produce. The lecture links this decision to the wants and preferences of individuals or groups, subject to limited resources. 每个经济体都必须决定生产哪些商品和服务。课件强调，生产内容受到个人或群体偏好影响，但同时受资源有限这一条件约束。 Example: A local government has a limited budget. If it builds a new sports centre, it may have fewer resources available for another public facility. 例子：地方政府预算有限。如果决定新建体育中心，就可能减少用于另一项公共设施的资源。 1.2 How to produce? | 如何生产？ Producers choose production methods based on the availability and relative cost of inputs. If workers are relatively cheaper than machines, a firm may use a more labour-intensive method. The lecture also notes that education can improve workers’ abilities and the quality of output. 生产者会根据生产要素是否充足、相对成本高低来决定生产方法。如果劳动力相对于机器更便宜，企业可能采用劳动密集型方式。课件还指出，教育能够提高劳动者的能力以及产品和服务的质量。 Example: A café can hire an extra worker to prepare drinks or purchase a machine that performs part of the preparation process. The relative costs and available resources affect the choice. 例子：咖啡店可以多雇一名员工制作饮品，也可以购买一台机器完成部分制作工作。两种方式的相对成本及资源条件会影响选择。 1.3 For whom to produce? | 为谁生产？ Economies must also determine who will receive the goods and services produced. The lecture highlights the role of income and raises the question of whether governments should intervene to promote more equitable outcomes. 经济体还必须决定生产出来的商品和服务由谁获得。课件强调收入的作用，并提出政府是否应通过干预市场促进更公平分配的问题。 Example: Two households may need similar housing, but their different incomes affect the type of accommodation they can afford. 例子：两个家庭可能都有住房需求，但由于收入不同，他们能够承担的住房类型也不同。 SOURCE • Lecture 2.1, pp. 5–8 2. Opportunity Cost and Trade-offs | 机会成本与取舍 Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made. The lecture stresses that this cost need not be measured in money: a sacrificed activity, benefit or output may be the real cost. 机会成本指作出一个选择时，被放弃的次优选择的价值。课件强调，机会成本不一定用金钱衡量；被放弃的活动、收益或产量都可能是真正的成本。 A trade-off means that gaining more of one thing requires giving up something else. The phrase “there is no such thing as a free lunch” reminds us that an apparently free option can still consume scarce time or resources. 取舍意味着多得到一样东西，往往需要放弃另一样东西。“天下没有免费的午餐”说明：即使某件事看起来不需要付钱，它也可能占用稀缺的时间或资源。 Example: You have two hours available. You can either attend an English speaking workshop or work on an economics assignment. If the workshop is your preferred option, studying economics has an opportunity cost equal to the benefit of the workshop you give up. 例子：你有两个小时，可以参加英语口语训练，也可以完成经济学作业。如果你原本更想参加口语训练，那么选择写经济学作业的机会成本就是放弃的口语训练收益。 KEY DISTINCTION | 关键区分 Opportunity cost is NOT the total value of every alternative you reject. It is the value of the single next best alternative. 机会成本不是你放弃的所有选择之和，而是其中最好的那个被放弃的选择的价值。 SOURCE • Lecture 2.1, pp. 10–11; Tutorial slides, pp. 8–10 3. PPC / PPF: A Model of Production Choices | 生产可能性曲线：解释生产选择的经济模型 An economic model is a simplified representation of reality. The Production Possibilities Curve (PPC), also called the Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), illustrates the maximum feasible combinations of two goods or categories of output that an economy can produce with its available resources and technology. 经济模型是对现实情况的简化。生产可能性曲线（PPC），也称生产可能性边界（PPF），表示经济体在现有资源和技术条件下，两种商品或两类产出的各种最大可实现生产组合。 3.1 PPC assumptions | PPC 的五项基本假设 Assumption / 假设 Meaning / 含义 Two outputs 仅考虑两类产出 Model focuses on two goods/categories. 模型只研究两类商品或产出。 Constant resources 资源数量固定 Available productive resources stay unchanged. 现有生产资源数量不变。 Constant technology 技术水平固定 Production methods and productivity do not change during the comparison. 比较期间技术和生产率不变。 Resources fully employed 充分就业 Frontier combinations use all available productive resources. 边界上的组合充分利用现有生产资源。 Resources transferable; ceteris paribus 资源可转移；其他条件不变 Resources can move between outputs; other factors are held constant. 资源可在两类产出间转移，其他因素保持不变。 Ceteris paribus means “other things remaining unchanged”. This assumption helps isolate the effect of a change in one variable. Ceteris paribus 意为“其他条件保持不变”。这种假设帮助我们单独分析一个变量变化带来的影响。 SOURCE • Lecture 2.1, pp. 14–16 3.2 The lecture’s consumer-goods/capital-goods schedule | 课件中的消费品—资本品组合 Point Consumer goods (C) Capital goods (K) E 120 0 I 90 30 N 40 55 A 0 60 Moving from point I (90 C, 30 K) to point N (40 C, 55 K) increases capital-goods production by 25 units but sacrifices 50 units of consumer goods. Exercise 1 Outline the concept of market equilibrium. Market equilibrium is a situation where price and output are determined through the processes of demand and supply. When the quantity demanded for a good or service equals the quantity supplied market equilibrium price and quantity occurs. At this point there is no tendency for change in either price or quantity. In Figure 1 the equilibrium price is OPe and the equilibrium quantity demanded and supplied is OQe given the existing market demand and supply situation. Exercise 2 Explain how market forces can combine to clear the market. In the event that there is a surplus of goods or services (where the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded) then firms will respond by cutting prices so that any surplus output is sold in the market. While ever the quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded prices will continue to fall and supply contract and consumers increasing the quantity demanded. Equilibrium will eventually occur at a lower price and a new equilibrium quantity. If there is a shortage of goods or services in the market (where the quantity supplied is less than the quantity demanded) then consumers will respond by pushing up prices by competing for the available quantity supplied of the good or service. Firms will respond by increasing the quantity supplied and this will occur while there continues to be a shortage. As the price charged for the 2 good or service rises the quantity supplied will increase as long as the shortage exists and consumer demand will in time contract. Equilibrium will eventually occur at a higher price and a new equilibrium quantity. Exercise 3 Explain how the government can use a price floor to maintain a minimum price in a market. Hint: Use appropriate terms, example/s and refer to the diagram in your response. A price floor occurs when the government establishes a minimum price that will be paid for a good or a service that is above the market equilibrium price. This ensures that the market price must not be allowed to go below the floor price. In Figure 1 above, the price floor occurs at OP1 which would stop the market price from falling below this level and reaching equilibrium at OPe. This price floor causes an excess of supply or surplus (AB) because the quantity supplied OQ2 will be greater than the quantity demanded OQ1. Generally, price floors are set to increase the income for producers of the goods or services that the government considers important, for example agricultural goods. Often these goods experience major changes (fluctuations) in prices because of the irregular supply conditions or due to overseas competition. Historically, the Australia government set a floor price for wool growers that aimed to support them by protecting their income when wool prices fluctuated. The other reason for a floor price was to protect some workers by setting a minimum wage (these workers are often less able to negotiate higher wages and/or are often less skilled than others). This minimum wage provided for a more equal distribution of income by maintaining the wages earned by lower income earners.

Because all economic activity revolves around the production of output (0), the earning of income (Y), and expenditure (E) it follows that economists are interested in the size of these aggregates, the relationships between them, and the reasons why they change. The circular flow of income model is a good starting point for understanding macroeconomic relationships. The circular flow model describes the continuous exchanges that occur in our modified market economy. SECTORS 1. The household sector (or consumers) includes all those who buy goods and services. T he household sector also provides the resources that go into the production of those goods and services. 2. The firms sector or (businesses) comprises all the units who employ the resources provided by households to produce the goods and services which are sold to consumers. 3. The financial sector comprises the firms which deal in financial services, including banks, building societies and other financial institutions. Not all of the income earned in the production process is spent (consumption). Most households choose to save some of their income. The financial sector forms a link between savers and investors. It acts as intermediaries between people or firms with surplus funds (S -savings) and those who wish to borrow them (I – investment). 4. The government sector (or public sector) consists of all government authorities at national, state and local level. Many important functions are provided by the government (G), which raises most of its revenue from taxation (T). 5. The overseas sector (or international sector) includes the rest of the world with whom our economy has economic relations by way of trade and financial flows. Domestic household and firms sectors spend some of their income overseas. Similarly, people in other countries buy domestic goods and services. Domestic goods and services sold overseas are called exports (X); goods and services which flow into our economy are known as imports (M). The difference between the two is called net exports. The production of goods and services by all sectors of the economy generates income for the people who contribute their effort and assets to that activity. Thus the income earned is equal to the value of goods and services produced. And in turn that income is used by consumers on spending, saving and taxes, and is subsequently used by firms and the government to pay employees to generate further income. Therefore we talk about the circular flow of income around the five sectors of the economy.

text: UNSW College Foundation Studies Economics Economics Unit 4 AGGREGATE DEMAND AND SUPPLY MODEL Learning Objectives : At the end of the unit you should able to : • Understand the economic determinants of the key expenditure components of aggregate demand in the economy • Develop an understanding of the aggregate demand – aggregate supply (AD– AS) macroeconomic model • Appreciate how the AD–AS macroeconomic model can be used to understand the business cycle and how macroeconomic policy can affect prices, GDP and employment Before this tutorial, you should have • Attended the Unit 4 lecture • Read ETF Textbook 7th Edition pages 349 - 365 • Read the Readings • Completed the Tutorial Questions During this tutorial, you will • Discuss/present your answers to the Tutorial Questions After this tutorial, you should • Consider attending one of the scheduled consultations and attempt to resolve any questions that you have as soon as possible Macroeconomics – Unit 4: Aggregate Demand and Supply Model Economics | Page 1 Readings AGGREGATE DEMAND AND AGGREGATE SUPPLY ANALYSIS The Aggregate demand/aggregate supply model ( or AD-AS model) can be used to explain the fluctuations in economic activity that take place during the business cycle. This model can show changes in the price level (i.e. inflation) and economic activity. Economic activity can be viewed in terms of the total (aggregate) level of demand and supply. As with demand and supply analysis in microeconomics, shifts in aggregate demand and aggregate supply in the economy will change the levels of output (GDP) growth, employment and prices (inflation). Aggregate Demand The curve slopes down from left to right i.e. as prices fall there is a rise in the aggregate quantity of goods and services demanded because: 1. As prices fall real income rises and therefore people can afford to buy an increased quantity of goods and services out of their money income. 2. As prices fall the country’s products become more competitive and easier to sell to other countries. The level of exports demand will increase. 3. Falling prices (lower inflation) allow interest rates to fall and therefore investment rises (increasing aggregate demand). Aggregate Supply The aggregate supply curve slopes upward from left to right i.e. as the level of supply increases the level of prices will rise. A rise in prices reduces the real wage, making production cheaper in real terms. Firms will be attracted to increase output as the general price level rises. As the economy approaches full capacity, in the short run, (the full employment level) resources become scarce. Resource prices will rise bringing inflation pressure to the economy. As the economy approaches full employment aggregate supply becomes less elastic : the curve becomes steeper becoming vertical at the full employment level of output. When the economy’s level of output falls, the aggregate supply curve becomes flat. The reason for this is that after a certain point prices will not fall significantly even if aggregate demand is shifting to the left. Resource prices may be “sticky” i.e. not falling. The fall in aggregate demand for resources (e.g. labour) may be reflected in lower employment rather than lower wages.

In doing so, we must keep in mind the special relationship between consumption and saving, since those factors which alter the level of household spending will also alter the level of household saving. Factors Affection Consumption The level of disposable income The level of disposable income is the key determinant of the level of consumption expenditure. In general, the higher the level of disposable income within the community, the higher is its level of household consumption. As total disposable income rises, of course, total household consumption increases. We can qualify this statement in two respects. Finally, let us note that it is quite possible (in the short run) for individual households to spend more than their current disposable incomes simply by borrowing or by drawing on their own past savings. This reduction in accumulated savings is called dissaving. The distribution of income If the distribution of income is uneven, households in upper income groups receive a relatively large proportion of total disposable income. The APC for these groups is relatively low (while their APS is relatively high). A more even distribution of income, on the other hand, means that households in the lower income groups receive a relatively larger share of total disposable income. Wealth It is often argued that, in the making their spending and saving decisions, households are heavily influenced by their levels of wealth. The term wealth basically refers to the total value of each household’s assets (cash, bank deposits, securities, and property such as cars and houses). (Notice that wealth and income are different concepts.) Given the same level of current disposable income, those households with accumulated wealth are more prepared to spend than those with little or no accumulated wealth. There are three reasons for this. Wealthy households: 1. have a greater capacity to borrow, since they can use their assets as collateral. 2. tend to have a greater volume of past savings on which they can draw. 3. are more likely to spend because their economic futures are relatively secure.

A central bank generally has the role of controlling a country’s money and banking system. As such, it is different from other banks – it is not set up as a financial business with the desire to make profit. Rather, its primary purpose is the overall management of the financial sector in accordance with the economic objectives of the Commonwealth Government. The RBA was created in 1959 under the Reserve Bank Act 1959. . According to the Reserve Bank’s Charter, in its conduct as Australia’s central bank, the Reserve Bank is to be guided by three broad objectives: • The stability of Australia’s currency • The maintenance of full employment • The economic prosperity and welfare of the people of Australia In reality, its highest priority in recent years has been to sustain low inflation or non- inflationary economic growth, Monetary policy involves action by the Reserve Bank (RBA) on behalf of the government, designed to influence the level of interest rates and the money supply. By influencing these variables, the RBA is also able to influence the overall level of economic activity in the short term and achieve medium to long term price stability. A change in the general level of interest rates will cause a change in the demand for credit. Higher interest rates will deter borrowing, whereas lower interest rates will encourage it. In the short term, tightening of monetary policy through increased interest rates will slow down economic activity. Higher interest rates will cause a reduction in consumer spending as consumers face higher costs for mortgages and consumer loans. Businesses also need to borrow to purchase new capital equipment. Higher interest rates will make borrowing more expensive so business investment will decline as well. The overall effect will be one of falling aggregate demand and slowing of economic activity. To boost aggregate demand and the level of economic activity the RBA would need to loosen monetary policy by reducing interest rates, which increases both consumer and business spending in the economy. A loosening of monetary policy would put downward pressure on interest rates, boosting consumer and investment spending, resulting in a higher level of economic activity, with falling unemployment, and an increase in inflationary pressures.

Macroeconomics – Unit 9: The Government Budget and Fiscal Policy Economics | Page 1 Readings The Public Sector Borrowing Requirement The “Public” sector refers to all 3 levels of government, as well as Government Business Enterprises, or Semi-Government Authorities ( Pacific Power, Telstra, Sydney Water etc ). * Where public sector revenue ( T ) is exceeded by expenditure ( G ) ( i.e. budget deficits ), government must finance this by raising loans, i.e. selling Treasury Notes and Bonds and other securities to the private sector. * The PSBR is the total amount of this loan raising by all governments each year. i.e. the annual borrowing requirement of the public sector, which adds to the Public Debt. * The PSBR is usually much greater than just the Federal Government Budget deficit. Therefore, a large Federal Government surplus is usually needed to bring PSBR to zero. The PSBR tends to push interest rates up and is said to “crowd out” private sector activity, including corporate investment in plant and equipment. Higher interest rates tend to attract overseas funds, raising the value of $A. This makes exports more expensive and imports cheaper, worsening our Trade balance. That portion of the PSBR financed by borrowing overseas also adds to the foreign debt. * The PSBR may also be inflationary and have a negative influence on business confidence. The Crowding Out Effect : Government economic activity is said to crowd out, or take the place of private sector activity, e.g. (i) government taxation reduces private consumption (ii) government spending demands goods, services and resources which are then unavailable for use by private sector (iii) government borrowing ( PSBR ) absorbs available savings funds and pushes interest rates up, which reduces private sector investment. Some economists believe that any level of government expenditure crowds out a significant amount of private sector activity and hence, government activity should be reduced.
